Who should use this specification

The intended readers of this specification are:

  • Application developers who want to create Java Micro Edition applications that use the Mobile User Interface Customization API to access user interface customization data

  • Implementers of the Mobile User Interface Customization API

How this specification is organized

This specification has three main parts:

  • Overview of the API and its implementation

  • The API reference

  • Appearance descriptor format description

The Overview part lists the goals and uses of the API, along with security considerations and implementation notes. The API Reference contains a complete listing of the classes and interfaces that belong to the API. The File Format Reference contains the formal definition of the appearance data file format used by implementations of this JSR.

Document conventions

The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "MAY" and "OPTIONAL" set in boldface type in this specification are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119 (see reference [Keywords]).

Monospaced type is used to denote literal text such as filenames and numeric constants, like filename.txt or 0x12345678, and symbolic constants such as KIND_GRAPHIC.

Customization concepts and common requirements

Overview

Introduction

This specification defines Mobile User Interface Customization API (JSR 258), a Java Micro Edition optional package that allows software developers to query and manipulate the appearance of a mobile device user interface, and introduces a common exchange format for appearance data, to be used by content developers and distributors.

Personal mobile devices are typically equipped with a graphical user interface. It provides a rich user experience, and in many devices it can also be customized. Users are able to change background images, color schemes, ringing tones and alert tones, and other features to their liking. Proprietary methods of grouping collections of customization settings and related content as "themes" have been established by device manufacturers, to enable end users to more easily change them in one operation.

The kind of user interface customization related to appearance described above has become increasingly popular as the graphics and sound capabilities of mobile devices have been greatly enhanced. Different user interface themes are used not only by individual users to personalize their devices, but also by telecommunications operators/carriers and device manufacturers to establish their brand and make the user experience more appealing, more seamless and more predictable in terms of appearance.

In addition to systemwide user interface customizations, also individual applications can often be customized to have a distinct look, using both application-specific user interface elements created by the application and customized appearances for system user interface elements.

Goals

The Mobile User Interface Customization API specification defines a standardized Java ME API for querying and manipulating themes and skins, and a file format for describing theme and skin data. It is intended for Java ME applications running on a combination of a Java ME configuration and a compatible profile with a graphical user interface.

The intent of the API specification is twofold: to define a Java API to query and manipulate theme and skin data on a mobile device, and to define a delivery format for the appearance definitions. Currently there is no common cross-platform theme or skin format in existence for mobile devices, nor is there a common Java API to access the content of themes and skins that exist in the device. Increasingly many devices have a Java Micro Edition (Java ME) implementation, and access to theme and skin data from a Java ME application is useful for application developers.

A high level model of Mobile User Interface Customization API operation

To be able to use the customization data and the Java API the device needs to support the concept of themes and skins in system software. If such support exists, then it is feasible for Java ME implementations of this API to use the native functionality to access theme and skin data.

The standard file format for describing theme and skin data as defined in this specification is intended to be used by device manufacturers, operators, application programmers and end users as the transportation and storage format for such data. This specification contains a formal definition of the file format. The format can be used without implementing the Java API.

Information about the appearance of user interface elements and the values of their customizable properties obtained with the API can be used to construct custom controls that blend well together with the user interface in terms of colors, backgrounds and other appearance features.

The customization data is intended to be usable widely across mobile devices and their operating systems, and also across different user interface toolkits and their selection of widgets.

Use cases

This section outlines the most common use cases for themes, skins and applications using the Mobile User Interface Customization API in a Java ME device.

Global appearance changes. The intent of themes is to change the appearance of the device user interface to something that is personally interesting to the user, or commercially viable as a promotion tool. This kind of device-wide customization is interesting to manufacturers, operators and end users alike. Using this API it is possible to programmatically change the currently active theme or its properties.

Application skinning. Developers of individual applications are able to provide alternative user interface appearances, freely selectable by the user. A collection of these could be shipped with the application or downloaded later.

Branding. Appearance customization has many possibilities for branding: corporate phones, operator look, chain store/retailer branding, movie themes as promotional giveaways (possibly using push technology), promotions of new operator services etc.

Regional/seasonal customization. Different world regions may require customization of the user interface without touching the application code. This could be achieved by providing a suitable appearance. New appearances can also be generated on a seasonal basis (celebration of summer/seasons greetings/harvest time etc.).

Portability of appearance definitions. An open and portable appearance definition format makes the same appearance definitions potentially usable in many different devices, thereby reducing the need to make custom versions of appearances to each different manufacturer’s device models.

Custom component development. The ability to query the properties of customizable elements in the user interface makes it possible to create custom components that blend better into the surrounding environment. For example, highlight and text color, background bitmaps and other properties can be queried and used when painting custom components (such as LCDUI CustomItems in MIDP, Component/JComponent subclasses in AGUI).

DRM protected content. For limited try-outs or subscription-based theme and skin services it is useful to be able to protect theme and skin definitions with Digital Rights Management (DRM) technology.

Concepts and terminology

This section introduces the domain-specific concepts and terminology used in this specification.

Themes and skins

The appearance of a mobile device user interface can be customized by applying user interface themes that describe the user interface visuals and trigger changes in their presentation. A theme is a collection of user interface customization data affecting the whole device. Themes are designed by content providers and made available for end users to download.

Individual applications can be customized in a different manner than the main user interface by applying skins, which are essentially themes specific to some application. Skins can be supplied with the application, and users can also download skins after the application is installed.

An application is said to be skinnable if its user interface can be customized independently of the surrounding system, by instructing it to use a different skin. These kinds of customizations are then specific to that application.

Collectively themes and skins are called appearances. This specification uses that term when referring to both themes and skins. In other cases the terms theme and skin are used explicitly.

The system default theme is the collection of default appearances for all the customizable elements supported by the implementation. It must have an appearance for every base element and for every toolkit element in all supported toolkits. If no theme is activated, the system default theme is in effect. When another theme is activated, some or all of the customizable elements MAY be overridden by the definitions in the activated theme.

Customizable elements

The targets of the customization are called customizable elements, which include features of the device user interface or an individual application's user interface, as well as widgets belonging to some specific user interface toolkit.

Examples of customizable elements on the device level (in the context of a mobile telephone) include the ring tone, the battery level indicator, the network strength indicator, the "wallpaper" or background image of the main screen and other such features. Customizing these base elements affects all applications in the device uniformly, inasmuch as those features are visible in the application's user interface or utilized by the application in custom widgets.

Similarly, on the level of widgets as found in some user interface toolkit examples include the list highlight, application background image, text color, text background color, and other such visual attributes. Customizing these toolkit elements affect applications that utilize the widgets from that user interface toolkit.

For the customization of elements that are specific to some application, skins can contain definitions of application elements that are neither base nor toolkit elements, but have semantics understood only by the application itself. Examples could include the control buttons of a media player (play, stop, pause, next track, previous track) or a browser (previous page, next page, stop, refresh), custom time displays and item highlights, among others.

A customizable element is either a standalone element with identifying attributes and element-specific content, or it is an element group that can in turn contain standalone elements or nested element groups.

Element kinds

Each customizable element has an associated kind, determined by its definition in the appearance descriptor file. The kind identifies the content of the element (for standalone elements) or indicates an element group.

Content kinds include media objects such as graphics, sounds and video, and simple values like integer, string and floating point values and ARGB color values. Constants for the different element kinds are defined in the Element interface.

Features and roles

Each customizable element has a feature attribute that determines the high-level classification of the element. Features are string values assigned by this specification or the appearance developer. Examples of features are "icon", "indicator" and "list".

In addition to a feature, each element also has a role attribute that identifies the element's function within the feature. Like features, roles are string values assigned by this specification or the appearance developer, such as "applicationDefault", "batteryStrength" and "itemHighlight".

Feature and role names do not generally convey enough meaning by themselves, but when combined, they accurately identify the purpose of the customizable element. For example, an element with the feature "icon" and the role "appdefault" could indicate that the element represents "the application default icon" (i.e. an icon assigned to applications by the system if they do not have a descriptive icon of their own). Similarly, an element with the feature "indicator" and the role "battery" could mean "the battery charge level indicator" found in the device user interface. The recommended semantics assigned to feature and role names are specified in the "Customizable elements" chapter of this specification (in the case of base and toolkit elements) or by the developer of the application and/or appearance (in the case of application specific elements as found in skins).

Base, toolkit and application elements

For both themes and skins, customizable elements in an appearance descriptor are grouped into a set base elements and possibly several sets of toolkit elements. Base elements are common to the device, while toolkit elements are specific to some user interface toolkit. These sets are disjoint in that they MAY contain elements with the same feature and role without any overriding.

Every implementation supports a well-determined set of base and toolkit elements. The supported base elements is the set of common customizable elements listed in the "File Format Reference" or a subset of it. The set of supported toolkit elements varies with the toolkit, but is expected to include elements from a recommended toolkit-specific set. For example, this specification contains a recommended set of customizable elements for LCDUI.

In practice this means that you could customize the list item highlight (feature="list", role="itemHighlight") using a base element, which would affect all list widgets in the device. If you then wanted to have a different list item highlight in LCDUI applications, you could achieve it using a toolkit element in the appropriate section, tagged with the same feature and role. These customizations would be distinct.

Additionally skins have a set of application elements, with semantics completely determined by the application. In implementations that support application-specific base and toolkit elements skins may have elements that override the active theme's base and toolkit elements.

File format

Customizations are defined using an appearance descriptor packaged together with any associated media objects inside an appearance container .

The "Appearance data file format" chapter in the "File Format Reference" part of this specification defines the format of the appearance descriptor that contains the customization information, expressed as an XML infoset which conforms to a schema. It also defines the transmission format of the appearance container.

Applications

In the context of this specification, an application is a Java ME application program running inside the Java Virtual Machine and depending on a configuration and a profile.

The Mobile User Interface Customization API implementation must associate application-specific skins with the right applications. This can be done using the application attribute of skins, independent of the application model used.

Customizable element lookup

This specification establishes a lookup order for the customizable elements. The order must be used by the implementation when an application requests information about an element.

In retrieving an element, what is actually looked for is a customization of the element. Eventually, if a customization for a certain element is not found, the default content of the element is returned, provided that the implementation supports the feature and role specified in the retrieval. If the feature and role combination is not supported, an ElementNotFoundException is thrown.

A reference to an appearance is always needed to retrieve an element. The element lookup must begin in the referred appearance. If a customization of the element with the specified feature and role is not found there, the lookup must proceed to the currently active skin of the application, if any. If a customization is not found in the active skin, the lookup must proceed to the currently active theme, if any. If a customization is not found in the active theme, the contents of the element must be retrieved from the system default theme. In each phase, if a customization is found, the lookup must end, returning a reference to the found element.

Customizable element lookup order

Note that this lookup order is applied to base and toolkit elements separately by the respective getElement and getToolkitElement methods. The lookup order does not apply to application elements in skins.

System requirements

This chapter contains information about the system requirements for the Mobile User Interface Customization API.

Configuration and profile

The Mobile User Interface Customization API is intended for Java Micro Edition implementations with the Connected, Limited Device Configuration (CLDC), version 1.1 or later, or the Connected Device Configuration (CDC), version 1.0.1 or later.

Specification compliance

A Mobile User Interface Customization API implementation is fully compliant if it:

  • Implements the mandatory parts of the API.

  • Can parse the appearance file format.

  • Can install appearances and select elements relevant to the device as described in the File Format Reference part, chapter "Appearance data file format", section "Context and element selection at installation time".

The implementation is file format compliant if it supports the file format like a fully compliant implementation but does not implement the API.

Mobile User Interface Customization API implementations MUST be either fully compliant or file format compliant. This implies that API implementations must also support the file format.

Optional API features

The following features of the API are optional:

  • Support for modify operations

  • Support for application-specific base and toolkit elements

Both of these are described in this section. All other features are mandatory.

Modify operations

Modify operations create new elements, themes or skins and update existing ones. In API compliant implementations the support for modify operations is OPTIONAL. This support is advertised to applications using the system property microedition.theme.modifysupported. If modify operations are supported, the value of this system property MUST be true, otherwise it MUST be false.

The modify operations are:

  • All ElementFactory methods

  • The updateElement, updateToolkitElement and commit methods of the Theme interface

  • The createTheme method of the ThemeManager class

  • The updateApplicationElement method of the Skin interface.

  • The createSkin method of the SkinManager interface

All of the optional methods must be present in the implementation to ensure binary compatibility. Implementations that do not support modify operations must throw a javax.microedition.theme.ModifyNotSupportedException immediately when any of the methods is called. This is also noted in the relevant method documentation.

Application-specific base and toolkit elements

The RELAX NG schema of the appearance descriptor allows skins to have base and toolkit sections. This is intended for implementations that can differentiate between the appearance of the user interface per application.

The support for application-specific base and toolkit elements is optional. This is reflected in the installation of skins so that the base and toolkit sections in application skins are discarded if the aforementioned support is not present. Details about the appearance installation process can be found in the File Format Reference.

The system property microedition.theme.applicationspecific can be used to determine if application-specific base and toolkit elements are supported by the implementation. If the feature is supported, the value of this system property must be true, otherwise it must be false.

System properties

The following table collects the system properties used in the Mobile User Interface Customization API. Detailed explanations of the properties appear below the table.

Table 1. System properties
Property name Description Value
microedition.theme.version Version number of the API implementation 1.0
microedition.theme.modifysupported Indicates support for modify operations true or false
microedition.theme.platform The implementation context name used in the context selection of appearances at installation time Implementation specific string in the same format as the name attribute in the context element of the appearance descriptor
microedition.theme.applicationspecific Indicates support for application-specific base and toolkit elements true or false

Version information

The version of Mobile User Interface Customization API is determined by the system property microedition.theme.version. If the device has an implementation of the API, this system property MUST be present, and its value MUST reflect the version number of the specification. For fully compliant implementations of version 1.0 (and 1.0.* maintenance releases) of this specification the value MUST be the string literal 1.0. File format compliant implementations MUST NOT have this system property, because it is intended for verifying the presence of the Java API.

Support for modify operations

The microedition.theme.modifysupported system property indicates whether the API implementation supports modify operations or not, as described in the "Optional features" section above. The value of this system property must be one of the string literals true and false.

Implementation context name (platform)

The microedition.theme.platform system property determines the implementation context name used when installing appearances, as explained in the "Context selection" section in the File Format Reference. The value of this system property is an implementation specific string literal, and it must be the same as the implementation context name.

Support for application-specific base and toolkit elements

The microedition.theme.applicationspecific system property indicates whether the API implementation supports application-specific base and toolkit elements or not, as described in the "Optional features" section above. The value of this system property must be one of the string literals true and false.

Installation and storage of appearances

Implementations of Mobile User Interface Customization API must have available an installation system and storage for appearances. This kind of subsystem typically already exists in platforms that have some kind of native support for themes and/or skins.

The responsibilities of the appearance management subsystem include at least the following:

  • Handling incoming transfers of appearance packages over the air or by other means;

  • Storing appearance data in an internal repository either in the file format described in this specification or in an optimized internal format, for accessing through the Java API;

  • Updating the internal appearance repository when appearances are added or removed by applications; and

  • Identifying and applying updates to themes already present in the repository.

Appearances can be installed using three different methods:

  • From a standalone application container, using the appearance management subsystem as outlined above;

  • Packaged together with an application in a JAR file; or

  • From a descriptor in the filesystem.

In each of these cases, the same rules for checking the appearance descriptor and the element definitions MUST be applied. These rules are described in the "File Format Reference" section of the specification.

Implementation notes

Implementations of this API SHOULD NOT handle the downloading of appearances into the device. Applications MUST be able to assume that when the API classes and methods are used, all themes and skins in the device are installed and ready for use.

The API does contain methods to delete existing appearances and to create new ones programmatically, subject to security restrictions. The result of these operations MUST be handled by the implementation together with the native appearance management application, so that the API clients have a consistent and up-to-date view of the appearance repository.

Security considerations

Changing the user interface appearance is not desirable in all circumstances, especially if it happens without the user's permission. To minimize disruption to the user, an implementation of the Mobile User Interface Customization API MUST limit customizations of the user interface in situations described later in this section.

Security policy

Java Micro Edition configurations and profiles have various security frameworks in place to protect the user from malicious applications. Implementations of this API MUST tie the functionality of the classes and methods to the appropriate security framework depending on the underlying configuration and profile.

In all the current Java Micro Edition security frameworks the restrictions are based on permissions that target specific API methods. In most cases applications have to request these permissions explicitly. This specification defines the permissions required to restrict access to certain security sensitive API methods. These permissions MUST be mapped to the security framework in effect in the runtime environment of the implementation.

The security sensitive methods and their associated permissions are listed in Appendix B, "Recommended Security Practices".

In all cases attempts to use a security sensitive API method without the appropriate permission MUST result in a java.lang.SecurityException being thrown.

Content protection policy

Complete appearance packages MAY be protected using Digital Rights Management (DRM) technology.

If DRM is implemented in the target device, implementations MAY install DRM protected appearances and allow partial programmatic access to them as detailed in this section.

For appearances installed from DRM protected appearance packages it MUST NOT be possible to retrieve any elements and their contents. Applications MAY be handed instances of DRM protected appearances, but only the metadata is accessible. It SHOULD be possible to activate DRM protected appearances programmatically, but it MUST NOT be possible to remove them. Any attempts to perform these operations MUST cause a java.lang.SecurityException to be thrown to the client.

If the usage rights of a DRM protected theme expire while the theme is active, the system default theme SHOULD be restored.

Device customization policy

Unlimited customization of all elements in the user interface is not always desirable or feasible. Implementations MAY restrict the customization of certain elements by providing a customization policy which denies programmatic appearance changes even if the corresponding method calls succeed in terms of security permissions.

The customization policy affects elements in themes and such skin elements that override any elements in the common set (as found in the "Common customizable elements" section).

If the programmatic customization of some element is denied by the customization policy, the implementation MUST throw a javax.microedition.theme.ElementNotCustomizableException from the method in question (typically updateElement).

In fully compliant implementations the state of any customization policy can be programmatically determined by calling the isCustomizationPolicyEnabled of the Capabilities class. Similarly, the customizability of individual base and toolkit elements can be determined by calling the relevant isElementCustomizable methods in the Capabilities and ToolkitCapabilities classes.

If the customization of some element is denied when installing one or more appearances from an appearance package, then that element MUST be discarded.

The customization policy MAY also limit customizations if the result would be a user interface that has its usability seriously degraded. This kind of "sanity checking" could involve detecting attempts to use white text on a white background, or similar cases. The extent of this checking is implementation dependent.

File Format Reference

Appearance data file format

This chapter contains the formal definition of the appearance container and the appearance descriptor. It also presents a sample appearance descriptor file containing many typical customization definitions.

The appearance container

The appearance container is a single archive file that holds inside it the appearance descriptor and all the files containing media objects that are referred to from the descriptor.

An appearance container that contains only a descriptor and related media files MUST be a JAR file (Java ARchive) conforming to the JAR File Specification (see reference [JAR]) and SHOULD have the extension .jar.

Appearances MAY also be deployed together with Java ME applications, inside the JAR file of the application. See the "Embedded appearances" section for details.

The internal organization and the locations inside the JAR file of the media objects related to appearances are dependent on the application that created the JAR file or inserted the appearance data inside it.

Media objects MUST be referred to from the descriptor using Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs as defined in RFC 2396, see reference [URI]). The following requirements apply to the URIs:

  • URIs MUST be relative to the location of the appearance descriptor.

  • URIs MUST NOT refer to resources outside the container.

  • URIs MUST be similarly relative also if the descriptor is extracted from the JAR into the file system.

  • The syntax of the URIs MUST conform to RFC 2396.

Manifest attributes

Manifest attributes in the JAR file are used to indicate the version of the Mobile User Interface Customization API required to handle the appearances, and to locate the appearance descriptor.

The MicroEdition-Theme-Version manifest attribute indicates the version of the Mobile User Interface Customization API the appearances are designed for. The value of this manifest attribute MUST match the value of the system property microedition.theme.version in fully compliant implementations. For example, appearances intended for implementations of version 1.0 of the API use the manifest attribute "MicroEdition-Theme-Version: 1.0". Note that the manifest attribute and the system property cannot be cross-checked in file format compliant implementations, because they are not required to have this system property defined. In this case the manifest attribute simply indicates the schema version.

The MicroEdition-Theme-Descriptor manifest attribute indicates the location and the filename of the appearance descriptor inside the JAR file. The location MUST be a relative URI starting from the root of the JAR. For example, if the descriptor file is called descriptor.xml and is located inside a directory named themes in the JAR root, the manifest attribute value is "MicroEdition-Theme-Descriptor: themes/descriptor.xml".

The appearance descriptor

The appearance descriptor is an application of XML 1.0 (see reference [XML]). The formal definition of the XML infoset is given as a RELAX NG schema (see reference [RELAXNG]). All compliant appearance descriptors MUST be well-formed XML and they SHOULD be valid according to the schema. For validation requirements, see the schema section below.

An appearance descriptor contains the definitions for the contents of customizable elements. The customization information is partitioned to themes and skins, which are further partitioned into different customization contexts.

The root element of the descriptor is appearance. The value of the version attribute of the root element must match the version number of the API implementation as reported by the microedition.theme.version system property.

Themes

Themes are intended for system-wide customization of a device's user interface. An appearance descriptor contains an arbitrary number of theme definitions, each with associated metadata and customizable elements.

Themes in the appearance descriptor contain one or more context sections to categorize the generic and platform specific customizations:

  • The generic customization context encapsulates generic cross-platform customizations. These are the customizable elements specified in Table 5, “The common customizable elements” of this specification. The generic context is identified by a name attribute with the value generic.

  • Platform customization contexts encapsulate optional platform specific customization definitions for elements that are supposed to be presented only in a specific platform. Platform specific contexts are identified by a name attribute with a platform specific value, such as s60rel3.

Context sections contain base and toolkit subsections to further categorize the customizable elements. Note that both of these sections MAY contain same elements, but they have a different mapping to the actual UI elements determined by the containing section:

  • The base section contains the definitions of the basic customizable elements. Usually these elements belong to the native user interface of the device, and correspond to the common customizable elements specified in Table 5, “The common customizable elements”.

  • The toolkit sections contain optional user interface toolkit specific customization definitions. These include elements which do not have a natural counterpart in the native user interface, such as some LCDUI-specific items in MIDP.

A conditionally mandatory set of these elements is defined in Table 5, “The common customizable elements”. The feature and role attributes in the context sections and their subsections MAY contain the same element names, as their meaning is interpreted by the containing section.

Skins

Skins are intended for the customization of the user interface of a specific application. An appearance descriptor MAY contain an arbitrary number of skin definitions, each with associated metadata and customizable elements. The customization information in the skin parts describe the user interface elements of the application, either standard elements in some toolkit or application-specific constructs.

Like themes, skins in the appearance descriptor contain one or more context sections. These sections MAY contain an application section for application-specific customization definitions.

Elements and element groups

Customizable elements are either single standalone elements (hereafter "elements") or element groups (hereafter "groups"). Both elements and groups are identified by a feature and a role attribute combination, which is unique within its containing section (that is, within base section and toolkit section) after the installation is completed. The most common feature and role attributes are defined in Table 5, “The common customizable elements”. In addition to those defined in this specification, an appearance descriptor MAY contain platform or application specific features and roles, but they MUST have a different feature and role than the common elements.

A group is composed of several elements or other groups. Elements and groups are identified by the feature and role of the group they belong to, and by the additional element-specific or group-specific feature and role identifying the element's or group's role within the containing group.

Variant elements

The base and toolkit sections MAY also contain variant elements or variants. They are differentiated by kind or media type, or both, and can be used to provide several alternative elements for a single customization. One of the variants MUST be selected during the installation of the appearance package.

The Mobile User Interface Customization API implementation MUST consider the variants in declaration order and use the first variant it can support (in terms of kind and media type). Other variants MUST be discarded.

Variants MUST NOT exist in the application section of a skin, because application specific customizations generally need not be varied across devices. They MAY, however, be used in other skin sections.

Presentation hints

Elements and groups MAY contain a presentation attribute for providing hints to the implementation on how to present some customizable element. The presentation attribute contains key/value pairs separated by a semicolon (U+003B), for example, presentation="opacity=75;fit=stretch;valign=middle;halign=center". The key/value pairs MAY be implementation specific. The key/value pairs defined in Table 2, “Set of common presentation hints” are conditionally mandatory, that is, their semantics MUST be understood by the Mobile User Interface Customization API implementation, if the underlying software platform supports applying that particular presentation directive to the customizable element.

Table 2. Set of common presentation hints
Key Conditionally mandatory values Description
opacity Value 0...100 The opacity of the element as a percentage (0 = fully transparent, 100 = fully opaque).
fit "stretch", "crop", "tile" The fit policy applied to the element's content within its containing element.
valign "top", "middle", "bottom" The vertical alignment policy of the element's content within its containing element.
halign "left", "center", "right" The horizontal alignment policy of the element's content within its containing element.
orientation "landscape", "portrait", "any" Indicates whether the element is intended to be shown only in the landscape or portrait mode of the device, or in both. If this hint is not specified, the default is "any" and the element is shown in both modes.

Toolkit names

The appearance descriptor allows toolkit sections to be labelled for use with some existing user interface toolkits. This specification defines canonical names for toolkits used in Java ME that exist at the time of writing. The following table lists the names to be used as values of the name attribute of a toolkit element.

Table 3. Canonical user interface toolkit names
Toolkit description Toolkit name
MIDP 2.0 LCDUI midp20lcdui
MIDP 2.1 LCDUI midp21lcdui
Personal Basis Profile 1.1 AWT pbp11awt
Personal Profile 1.1 AWT pp11awt
eSWT 1.0 eswt10
AGUI (JSR 209) agui10

It is RECOMMENDED that when a new user interface toolkit for Java ME is defined, it specifies a value to be used for this same purpose, so that it can be used in conjunction with the Mobile User Interface Customization API.

Attribute value syntax restrictions

Attribute values in theme and skin definitions MUST conform to the XML specification. The following additional restrictions MUST be applied to the attribute values. When appropriate, these restrictions are enforced by the RELAX NG schema. This documentation is intended for implementations that do not validate the perform in-device validation of the appearance descriptors against the RELAX NG schema.

Table 4. Attribute value restrictions

Restriction XML element Attribute or data Notes
ASCII lowercase (U+0061 to U+007A inclusive), ASCII uppercase (U+0041 to U+005A inclusive), numerals 0...9 (U+0030 to U+0039 inclusive), dot (U+002E) element feature, role Case-insensitive
theme, skin name, version, vendor Case-insensitive
Like name, version, vendor, with the addition of colon (U+003A) skin application Case-insensitive
URI (RFC 2396) element, icon src  
MIME type (RFC 2045) element, icon type  
Color (AARRGGBB) element value Element kind must be color
Date (ISO 8601:1988) created, modified (data) See XML Schema datatype
Language tag (RFC 3066) title, description xml:lang See XML Schema datatype
texts default See XML Schema datatype
Presentation hint: like name, version, vendor, with the addition of semicolon (U+003B) and equals sign (U+003D) element presentation Case-insensitive
Font specification: like name, version, vendor, with the addition of space (U+0020) and vertical line (U+007C) element value Element kind must be font


More specific restrictions are detailed below.

Theme and skin identification

Themes and skins are identified by the name, version and vendor attributes. Additionally skins have an application attribute that identifies the application they are intended for.

The version attribute must have a major and minor version number separated by a dot (U+002E), for example "1.0".

The vendor attribute must be the reverse domain name of the theme or skin vendor, for example "com.nokia".

Note that the author and vendor attributes have different semantics and are not necessarily the same.

The identifier values are restricted to ASCII because they are intended to be used as internal to the application, not to be displayed to the user.

Application and skin matching

The application attribute of the skin element is used to match skins and applications at runtime. Each skin is stored with information about the application that the skin is intended for, in the form of a name/version/vendor triplet. Note that these values are distinct from the skin's attributes of the same name.

The value of the application attribute must be expressed as a single string of the format "appName:appVersion:appVendor". The values must match the argument of the getInstance method of the SkinManager class. See the sample appearance descriptor and the code examples for details.

Color values

Attribute values that represent ARGB color values MUST be a named color or a numeric constant of the form #AARRGGBB, where the components AA, RR, GG and BB are 8-bit values expressed as hexadecimal constants. AA is the opacity level, and RR, GG, BB are the red, green and blue levels respectively. Named colors MUST be recognized color keywords as found in the SVG 1.1 specification (see reference [SVG11]). Examples: #FFCC6633, lightskyblue.

For the alpha values, 00 = fully transparent and FF = fully opaque. Intermediate values specify semitransparency. If the implementation does not support transparency for certain element, the alpha values MUST be ignored and the color value MUST be treated as completely opaque.

Other values

Attribute values that represent URIs MUST conform to RFC 2396 (see reference [URI]).

Date attribute values in the metadata MUST be ISO 8601:1988 dates (see reference [ISO8601]).

The title and description attributes are localizable with the xml:lang attribute. The value of the xml:lang attribute MUST conform to RFC 3066 (see reference [LangTags]). The default attribute of the texts element MUST also conform to RFC 3066.

Attribute value semantic restrictions

Theme names

Theme names MUST be strings of the form "name:version:vendor", where name, version and vendor correspond to the name, version and vendor attribute values of the theme element in the descriptor.

Each theme name MUST be unique within the scope of the appearance descriptor, i.e. one descriptor cannot contain more than one theme with the same name.

Any theme in the descriptor MUST NOT have a name that corresponds to the value of the SYSTEM_DEFAULT_THEME constant in the ThemeManager class.

Skin names

Skin names MUST be constructed like theme names.

Each skin name MUST be unique within the scope of one application element, i.e. there cannot be two skins with the same name intended for the same application.

Application names

Application names are used to identify an application for the purposes of connecting applications and their skins. They are strings of the form "appName:appVersion:appVendor", matching the value of the application of the skin element.

Installing appearances

This section gives information about the checks that MUST be performed on the appearance data when an appearance package is installed in the device. The original descriptor file MAY be retained after the installation.

The implementation SHOULD reject the appearance descriptor if it is not well-formed as defined by the XML 1.0 specification. If the implementation validates the appearance descriptor against the RELAX NG schema, it SHOULD reject the descriptor if it does not conform to the schema. If a descriptor is rejected, the user MUST be informed.

Context selection

An appearance definition MAY contain several contexts. They MAY have nested contexts, except for the context with the name attribute value "generic", which MUST NOT contain other contexts.

The Mobile User Interface Customization API implementation MUST define a context name that is used to identify the context that applies to that particular implementation. This name, later referred to as the implementation context name, is used to select the appropriate elements.

When an appearance package is installed, the Mobile UI Customization API implementation MUST select the appropriate contexts and customization definitions for the device, according to the following rules:

  • The context with the name attribute value "generic" MUST always be selected for processing.

  • If there is a context with a name attribute value that corresponds to the implementation context name, then that context and all its parent contexts up to the topmost one in the context element MUST be selected for processing. Other nested contexts inside that context must be discarded.

When the relevant contexts have been selected, they MUST be checked for overlapping element definitions. In case of nested contexts, if the parent context and child context contain elements with the same feature and role, the element in the child overrides the element in the parent.

Similarly, if the generic context and the implementation context contain elements with the same feature and role, the platform element definition overrides the generic element definition.

If some context contains two or more elements with the same feature and role, and they are not variant elements, the first supported element is selected and the others are discarded. However, note that after the processing the base and toolkit sections remain, and they MAY contain elements with the same feature and role.

If there are toolkit sections which refer to unsupported user interface toolkits, they MUST be discarded.

After the rules above have been applied, there remains a single list of customizable elements that has no specific context. The notion of context thus applies only at installation time, and is not reflected in the runtime API.

The following example illustrates the context selection. It contains a fragment of an appearance descriptor with nested contexts. 

<context name="generic">
    <element feature="A" role="B" ...>  <!-- (1) -->
    <element feature="C" role="D" ...>  <!-- (2) -->
</context>

<context name="S60Rel3">
    <context name="NokiaS60">
        <context name="NokiaN91">
            <element feature="A" role="B" ...> <!-- (3) -->
        </context>
    </context>    
</context>

Assuming that the implementation context name is "NokiaN91", the selected elements are 2 and 3. Element 1 is not selected because it is overridden by element 3, which has the same feature and role.

Element checking

When the context has been resolved, the remaining list of customizable elements MUST be subjected to media type and kind checking, according to the following rules:

  • (For skins only:) If application-specific base and toolkit elements are not supported by the implementation, the base and toolkit sections in the skin must be discarded.

  • If the feature or role specified in the element definition is the empty string, the element MUST be discarded.

  • If the feature and role combination in the element definition is not supported by the implementation, the element MUST be discarded. This check MUST be performed separately for the base elements and the toolkit elements in the appearance, using the relevant information about supported elements as reported by the implementation.

  • If the kind or media type in the element definition is not supported by the implementation for the specified feature and role combination, the element MUST be discarded. If the element to be discarded belongs to a group, the whole group MUST be discarded, up to the top level.

Note that these checks MUST NOT be applied to elements in the application section of a skin. They MAY have elements with media types or feature and role combinations unknown to the implementation.

Finally, if there is a customization policy currently in effect, it MUST be consulted for all the remaining elements except the elements in a skin's application section. Elements which are not customizable according to the policy MUST be discarded. More information about the policy can be found in the "Device customization policy" section.

If the appearance has no elements, either originally or because of the installation-related checks, the user should be prompted and given the possibility to cancel the installation of that appearance.

Embedded appearances

Applications to be installed to the device may have embedded appearances. These must be processed by compliant Mobile User Interface Customization API implementations.

When a device receives a JAR file with the manifest attribute MicroEdition-Theme-Descriptor, the implementation must check for the MicroEdition-Theme-Version manifest attribute. In fully compliant implementations the value of this attribute MUST match the value of the microedition.theme.version system property. In file format compliant implementations the equivalent information MUST be stored by the implementation.

If the implementation determines it can support the appearance version, it MUST attempt to parse the file as an appearance descriptor according to this specification.

If successful, the implementation MUST store the processed customization data in the device so that the data is available through the Mobile User Interface Customization API. The implementation SHOULD prompt for the user's approval before installing the appearances.

If an error occurs during the installation, an appropriate localized error message SHOULD be shown to the user and the appearance data MUST be rejected. Retaining the original appearance data after a successful installation is OPTIONAL.

The implementation should ensure that any successful installation of embedded appearances is finished before the application installation. This avoids a situation where an application could be started but the appearances bundled with it would not yet be available.

Removing appearances

When an application is removed, the implementation must check for skins related to the application. If any skins are found, they should be deleted when the application is removed, provided that the user has been queried. If the user does not allow it, the skins must not be deleted.

If any themes were installed along with an application, the implementation should not offer to remove them, because the user most likely wants to use them even after the application has been removed.

The RELAX NG schema

This section describes the RELAX NG schema for the appearance descriptor. Implementations of the Mobile User Interface Customization API MAY validate the appearance descriptor, but it is NOT RECOMMENDED for performance reasons. However, RELAX NG schema validation is better suited for performance-constrained mobile devices than XML Schema validation.

Implementations of tools that generate Mobile User Interface Customization API compliant appearance definition files MUST validate the appearance descriptors they generate. If the tool does not does not support RELAX NG, it is possible to generate an equivalent XML Schema from the RELAX NG schema using a suitable utility program such as Trang by James Clark.

The RELAX NG schema of the appearance descriptor follows:

<?xml version="1.0"?>

<grammar ns="http://www.jcp.org/jsr258/ns/theme/1.0" 
         xmlns="http://relaxng.org/ns/structure/1.0" 
         datatypeLibrary="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-datatypes">
    <!-- Using the XML Schema datatype library for basic datatypes
         like language and date. -->
                  
    <!-- Define the document root element -->
    <start>
    
        <!-- 
            Appearance element containing the themes and skins.
            The "version" attribute must match the version of the 
            Mobile User Interface Customization API specification.
        -->
        <element name="appearance" ns="http://www.jcp.org/jsr258/ns/theme/1.0">
            <attribute name="version" />
            
            <!-- Start of theme definition -->
            <!-- An appearance contains zero or more themes -->
            <!-- A theme is identified by name, version and vendor attributes -->
            <zeroOrMore>
                <element name="theme">
                    <attribute name="name" />
                    <attribute name="version" />
                    <attribute name="vendor" />
                    <!-- A theme contains a metadata section -->
                    <element name="themeinfo">
                        <ref name="metadata" />
                    </element>
                    
                    <!-- A theme contains one or more context sections -->
                    <oneOrMore>
                        <ref name="themecontext" />
                    </oneOrMore> <!-- context -->
                    
                </element>  <!-- theme -->
            </zeroOrMore> <!-- theme -->
            <!-- End of theme definition -->
            
            <!-- Start of skin definition -->
            <!-- An appearance contains zero or more skins -->
            <!-- A skin is identified by name, version and vendor attributes -->
            <zeroOrMore>
                <element name="skin">
                    <attribute name="name" />
                    <attribute name="version" />
                    <attribute name="vendor" />
                    <attribute name="application" />
        
                    <!-- A skin contains a metadata section -->
                    <element name="skininfo">
                        <ref name="metadata" />
                    </element>
                    
                    <!-- A skin contains one or more context sections -->
                    <oneOrMore>
                        <ref name="skincontext" />
                    </oneOrMore> <!-- context -->
                    
                </element> <!-- skin -->
            </zeroOrMore> <!-- skin -->
            <!-- End of skin definition -->
        </element> <!-- appearance -->
    </start>

    <!-- Define named patterns referred to from the start element -->
        
    <!-- Definition of metadata block for themes and skins -->
    <define name="metadata">
        <ref name="texts" />
        <ref name="author" />
        <element name="created">
            <data type="date" />
        </element>
        <element name="modified">
            <data type="date" />
        </element>
        <optional>
            <ref name="icon" />
        </optional>
    </define>
    
    <define name="texts">
        <element name="texts">
            <!-- 
                The "default" attribute is the default locale of the text.
                The value is an RFC 3066 tag like the "xml:lang" attributes
                in the title and description elements.
            -->
            <attribute name="default" />

            <!-- title and description are localizable -->
            <oneOrMore>
                <element name="title">
                    <attribute name="xml:lang">
                        <data type="language" /> <!-- RFC 3066 tag -->
                    </attribute>
                    <text />
                </element>
            </oneOrMore>
            
            <oneOrMore>
                <element name="description">
                    <attribute name="xml:lang">
                        <data type="language" /> <!-- RFC 3066 tag -->
                    </attribute>
                    <text />
                </element>
            </oneOrMore>
            
        </element> <!-- texts -->
    </define>
    
    <define name="author">
        <element name="author">
            <text />
        </element>
    </define>
    
    <define name="icon">
        <element name="icon">
            <attribute name="src">
                <data type="anyURI" />
            </attribute>
            <attribute name="type" />
        </element>
    </define>
    
    <!-- Theme context -->
    <define name="themecontext">
        <element name="context">
            <attribute name="name" />
            
            <!-- Context in a theme has zero or one base section -->
            <optional>
                <element name="base">
                    <oneOrMore>
                        <ref name="elementOrGroupOrVariant" />
                    </oneOrMore>
                </element>
            </optional>
            
            <!-- Context in a theme has zero or more toolkit sections -->
            <zeroOrMore>
                <element name="toolkit">
                    <attribute name="name" />
                    <oneOrMore>
                        <ref name="elementOrGroupOrVariant" />
                    </oneOrMore>
                </element>
            </zeroOrMore>
            
            <!-- Recursive reference to themecontext -->
            <zeroOrMore>
                <ref name="themecontext" />
            </zeroOrMore>
            
        </element> <!-- context -->
    </define> <!-- themecontext -->
    
    <!-- Skin context -->
    <define name="skincontext">
        <element name="context">
            <attribute name="name" />
            
            <!-- Context in a skin has zero or one application section -->
            <optional>
                <element name="application">
                    <oneOrMore>
                        <ref name="elementOrGroup" />
                    </oneOrMore>
                </element>
            </optional>
            
            <!-- Context in a skin has zero or one base section -->
            <optional>
                <element name="base">
                    <oneOrMore>
                        <ref name="elementOrGroupOrVariant" />
                    </oneOrMore>
                </element>
            </optional>
            
            <!-- Context in a skin has zero or more toolkit sections -->
            <zeroOrMore>
                <element name="toolkit">
                    <attribute name="name" />
                    <oneOrMore>
                        <ref name="elementOrGroupOrVariant" />
                    </oneOrMore>
                </element>
            </zeroOrMore>
            
            <!-- Recursive reference to skincontext -->
            <zeroOrMore>
                <ref name="skincontext" />
            </zeroOrMore>
            
        </element> <!-- context -->
    </define> <!-- skincontext -->
    
    <!-- Standalone element or an element group or variant group in theme or skin -->
    <define name="elementOrGroupOrVariant">
        <choice>
            <ref name="standaloneElement" />
            <ref name="elementGroup" />
            <ref name="variantGroup" />
        </choice>
    </define>
    
    <!-- Standalone element or an element group in the application specific 
         section of a skin -->
    <define name="elementOrGroup">
        <choice>
            <ref name="standaloneElement" />
            <ref name="elementGroup" />
        </choice>
    </define>
    
    <!-- Standalone element -->
    <define name="standaloneElement">
        <element name="element">
            <!-- standalone element always has both feature and role -->
            <ref name="featureAndRoleAttributes" />
            <ref name="kind" />
            <!-- (type src) | value -->
            <choice>
                <ref name="typeAndSrcAttributes" />
                <attribute name="value" />
            </choice>
            <ref name="presentation" />
        </element>
    </define>
    
    <!-- Feature and role go together -->
    <define name="featureAndRoleAttributes">
        <group>
            <attribute name="feature" />
            <attribute name="role" />
        </group>
    </define>
    
    <!-- Type and src go together -->
    <define name="typeAndSrcAttributes">
        <group>
            <attribute name="type" />
            <attribute name="src" />
        </group>
    </define>
    
    <!-- Presentation attribute -->
    <define name="presentation">
        <optional>
            <attribute name="presentation" />
        </optional>
    </define>
    
    <!-- Kind attribute -->
    <define name="kind">
        <attribute name="kind">
            <choice>
                <value>graphic</value>
                <value>sound</value>
                <value>video</value>
                <value>color</value>
                <value>integer</value>
                <value>float</value>
                <value>string</value>
                <value>font</value>
            </choice>
        </attribute>
    </define>
    
    <!-- An element group with elements and/or groups inside -->
    <define name="elementGroup">
        <element name="group">
            <ref name="featureAndRoleAttributes" />
            <ref name="presentation" />
            <zeroOrMore>
                <ref name="standaloneElement" />
            </zeroOrMore>
            <!-- Recursive reference to elementGroup -->
            <zeroOrMore>
                <ref name="elementGroup" />
            </zeroOrMore>
        </element>
    </define>
    
    <!-- A variant group with at least one variant specific element or group -->
    <define name="variantGroup">
        <element name="variant">
            <ref name="featureAndRoleAttributes" />
            <oneOrMore>
                <choice>
                    <ref name="standaloneVariantElement" />
                    <ref name="variantElementGroup" />
                </choice>
            </oneOrMore>
        </element>
    </define>
    
    <!-- Standalone variant element -->
    <define name="standaloneVariantElement">
        <element name="element">
            <!-- Standalone variant element has no feature or role -->
            <ref name="kind" />
            <ref name="presentation" />
            <!-- (type src) | value -->
            <choice>
                <ref name="typeAndSrcAttributes" />
                <attribute name="value" />
            </choice>
        </element>
    </define>
    
    <!-- A variant element group with elements and/or groups inside -->
    <define name="variantElementGroup">
        <element name="group">
            <!-- Variant element group never has feature nor role -->
            <ref name="presentation" />
            <zeroOrMore>
                <ref name="standaloneElement" />
            </zeroOrMore>
            <!-- Recursive reference to elementGroup 
                 (note: not variantElementGroup!), so that the feature 
                 and role are allowed in the nested groups -->
            <zeroOrMore>
                <ref name="elementGroup" />
            </zeroOrMore>
        </element>
    </define>
    
</grammar>

Sample appearance descriptor

A sample appearance descriptor conforming to the RELAX NG schema follows:

<?xml version="1.0"?>
<?oxygen RNGSchema="appearance.rng" type="xml"?>
<appearance version="0.20" xmlns="http://www.jcp.org/jsr258/ns/theme/1.0">

    <theme name="BlueSky" version="1.0" vendor="com.acme">
        <themeinfo>
            <!-- 
                Title and description elements with several locale dependent 
                alternatives. The xml:lang attribute values must conform to 
                RFC 3066.
            -->
            <texts default="en">
                <title xml:lang="en">My Blue Sky Theme</title>
                <title xml:lang="fi">Sininen Taivas Teema</title>
                <description xml:lang="en">Description in English
                here.</description>
                <description xml:lang="fi">Kuvaus suomeksi.</description>
            </texts>
            <author>Acme Corporation</author>
            <created>2005-08-15</created>  <!-- must be ISO 8601:1988 date -->
            <modified>2006-04-10</modified>
            <icon type="image/png" src="blueskyicon.png" />
        </themeinfo>
        
        <!-- Section for all generic cross-platform customizations --> 
        <context name="generic">
            <base>
                <!-- A default icon for applications -->
                <element feature="icon" role="applicationDefault"
                    kind="graphic" type="image/png" src="appicon.png" />
                    
                <!-- General wallpaper for idle screen background -->
                <element feature="idleScreen" role="background"
                    kind="graphic" type="image/jpeg" src="blueskywallpaper.jpg" />
                
                <!-- Status area background -->
                <element feature="statusArea" role="background"
                    kind="graphic" type="image/bmp" src="statusbg.bmp" />
                    
                <!-- Application main area background -->
                <element feature="mainArea" role="background"
                    kind="graphic" type="image/svg+xml" src="idle.svg"
                    presentation="opacity=75;valign=center;halign=center" />
                
                <!-- Softkey area background -->
                <element feature="softkeyArea" role="background"
                    kind="graphic" type="image/bmp" src="bgctrl.bmp" />
                    
                <!-- 
                    Example of two alternative media objects for a ringtone. 
                    If the implementation cannot support MP3 ringtones then 
                    the MIDI file is selected instead. 
                -->
                <variant feature="tone" role="ringing">
                    <element kind="sound" type="audio/mpeg" src="flyingsong.mp3" />
                    <element kind="sound" type="audio/midi" src="flyingsong.mid" />
                </variant>
                
                <!-- 
                    Example of two alternative kinds for the list highlight.
                    If the implementation cannot support a graphics file as the
                    highlight then a solid color value is used instead. 
                -->
                <variant feature="list" role="itemHighlight">
                    <element kind="graphic" type="image/svg+xml"
                        src="roundedrect.svg" />
                    <element kind="color" value="#FFFF2288" />
                </variant>
                
            </base>
            
            <!-- 
                Cross-platform customizations for MIDP 2.0 LCDUI.
                The features and roles are from the recommended list
                of LCDUI customizable elements in the specification. 
            -->
            <toolkit name="midp2lcdui">
                <element feature="list" role="background"
                    kind="graphic" type="image/jpeg" src="midplistbg.jpg" />
                <element feature="list" role="itemHighlight"
                    kind="graphic" type="image/png" src="midplisthl.png" />
                <element feature="item" role="border"
                    kind="color" value="#FF445566" />
                <element feature="item" role="highlightedBorder"
                    kind="color" value="#FFFFFFFF" />
                <element feature="item" role="background"
                    kind="color" value="#FF000000" />
                <element feature="item" role="highlightedBackground" 
                    kind="color" value="#FF000000" />
                <element feature="item" role="foreground"
                    kind="color" value="#FFFFFFFF" />
                <element feature="item" role="highlightedForeground" 
                    kind="color" value="#FFAFAFAF" />
            </toolkit>
        </context>
        
        <!-- 
            Platform specific customizations. The semantics of the
            features and roles are specific to the platform implementation. 
        -->
        <context name="S60Rel3">
            <base>
                <!-- An icon with multiple images -->
                <group feature="icon" role="shell">
                    <element feature="icon" role="shellicon" 
                        kind="graphic" type="image/bmp" src="shellicon.bmp" />
                    <element feature="icon" role="shelliconmask1"
                        kind="graphic" type="image/bmp" src="shelliconmask1.bmp" />
                    <element feature="icon" role="shelliconmask2"
                        kind="graphic" type="image/bmp" src="shelliconmask2.bmp" />
                </group>
                
                <!-- Icons with single images -->
                <element feature="icon" role="bluetooth"
                    kind="graphic" type="image/svg+xml" src="bticon.svg" />
                <element feature="icon" role="calendar"
                    kind="graphic" type="image/svg+xml" src="calicon.svg" />
                <element feature="icon" role="messaging"
                    kind="graphic" type="image/svg+xml" src="msgicon.svg" />
                
                <!-- 
                    Example of a battery charge level indicator that consists
                    of three images, expressed as an element group. 
                -->
                <group feature="indicator" role="batterystrength">
                    <element feature="frame" role="bottom"
                        kind="graphic" type="image/jpeg" src="battery_bottom.jpg" />
                    <element feature="frame" role="middle"
                        kind="graphic" type="image/jpeg" src="battery_middle.jpg" />
                    <element feature="frame" role="top"
                        kind="graphic" type="image/jpeg" src="battery_top.jpg" />
                </group>                    
            </base>
        </context>
    </theme>

    <!-- 
            MediaPlayer application skins 
    -->
    <skin application="MediaPlayer:1.0:com.nokia" 
          name="Gargoyle" version="0.1" vendor="com.acme">
        <skininfo>
            <texts default="en">

        <context name="generic">
            <!--

            <application>
                <element feature="transportbar" role="background"
                    kind="graphic" type="image/png" src="greenbar.png" />

            <!--

                    kind="graphic" type="image/png" src="mplisthighlight.png" />
            </toolkit>
        </context>
    </skin>

</appearance>

Customizable elements

This chapter defines the typical user interface elements which are customizable using the Mobile User Interface Customization API.

The customizable elements are identified by the feature and role attributes. Their values MUST be case-insensitive. The attribute values defined in Table 5, “The common customizable elements” use "camel-casing" for better readability. The values MUST be strings which conform to the attribute value syntax restrictions as found in the "Appearance Descriptor" section.

Common customizable elements

This section contains a list of the common customizable elements, and their corresponding features and roles. This set of elements is conditionally mandatory in all Mobile User Interface Customization API implementations, i.e. if the underlying software platform supports the customization of a certain element, then customization of that element MUST be supported also by the Mobile User Interface Customization API implementation.

It is RECOMMENDED that implementations map these common elements internally to any similar native elements available in the platform.

It is recommended that elements represented by a nine-part graphic, such as areas and highlights, are implemented as follows:

  • The nine-part graphic is expressed as an element group with the individual graphics as group members

  • The roles of the member elements are assigned as topleft, top, topright, right, bottomright, bottom, bottomleft, left and center, as the role names indicate

  • The order of the elements inside the group is irrelevant

Platform-specific customizable elements

If there is more than one element with the same feature and role in the same appearance definition but within different contexts, the element selected is resolved using the rules in the "Context selection" section. For platform-specific customizable element definitions which are not intended to override any of the common customizable elements, use a feature name that does not appear in the common element list. It is RECOMMENDED that the feature name is prefixed at least with the reverse domain name of the platform vendor. This ensures that the element does not override a common customizable element with the same feature and role.

Element kinds and media types

Most customizable elements have a naturally matching element kind that should be used by the implementation. This kind is the one that most closely matches the semantics of the element. For example, icons are expected to be bitmap images or SVG files, not integers or strings. The kind used for each element is implementation-dependent, and MUST be reported correctly to applications through the methods in the Capabilities and ToolkitCapabilities classes.

In terms of media types, most customizable elements are "polymorphic" in the sense that the same element can hold a separate content type in different implementations. For example, some implementations support a nine-part element group of bitmap images as the higlight for a list item, whereas other implementations could allow an SVG graphic.

The following table lists the mandatory and optional content types that MUST be supported for each kind of customizable element.

For other element kinds besides simple values, the mandatory and optional types are the registered MIME types for the appropriate graphic, sound and video formats.

Mandatory types MUST be supported by all implementations. If the device has native support for some optional media type, then that media type SHOULD be supported.

Table 6. Kinds of elements and their associated content types
Kind of element Mandatory types Optional types Usage examples
graphic JPEG image, GIF image, PNG image SVG Tiny, M3G Foreground images, animations, ornamental images, icons, wallpapers, widget background images, highlights in input and selection elements, indicators
sound MIDI, SP-MIDI Mobile XMF, MP3, AAC, AMR-WB, audio/x-tone-seq Ringtones, alert tones, activity tones
video 3GPP MPEG-4, Real Media Video clips
color ARGB color value Color names as found in the SVG specification Individual color values
number Integer or floating point number - Counts, measurements
string Display text or enumerated value - Text shown in the user interface or used as a feature identifier
font Font information in the format font-family;font-style;font-size (see below) Complete font designations (font used as is or mapped to some other font in the system)

The format of the font information MUST include the font family name, the font style flags and the font size in pixels, separated by a semicolon (U+003B). The font style flags consist of the values plain, bold, italic and underlined, separated by a vertical bar (U+007C). Some examples of font information attribute values are Arial;bold;8 and Times;bold|italic;12. The styles correspond exactly to those defined in MIDP 2.0 (see [MIDP2]).

The font information MAY be used directly by the system to select some font, or it MAY be mapped to some other equivalent font in the system. The mapping is implementation dependent.

Recommended toolkit specific customizations

This section lists the elements that SHOULD be customizable in specific user interface toolkits that are currently widely deployed.

Any new user interface toolkits SHOULD define similar bindings. If the Mobile UI Customization API is implemented in a device together with this kind of new toolkit, the interoperability of the implementation is greatly increased by such bindings.

MIDP 2.0 LCDUI

This section lists the recommended customizations in the LCDUI of MIDP 2.0 (JSR 118, see reference [MIDP2]), which SHOULD be customizable in devices that have implementations of both the Mobile User Interface Customization API and MIDP 2.0. These recommendations also apply to MIDP 2.1.

Glossary

appearance

a collective term for themes and skins

appearance container

a JAR file that contains an appearance descriptor and the media objects referred to from the descriptor

appearance definition file

part of an appearance descriptor that defines a theme or a skin

appearance descriptor

the XML infoset that describes elements to be customized in some appearance, together with their contents

application

a Java ME application program running inside the Java Virtual Machine and depending on a configuration and a profile

application-specific base and toolkit elements

a feature of the implementation that supports different renderings of base and toolkit elements for different applications

application element

a customizable element specific to some application, and is not a base element or a toolkit element

application name

identifying string for the application in the format appName:appVersion:appVendor

base element

a customizable element that belongs to the native user interface of the device

context

a grouping of customizable element definitions applicable to a certain platform or model

customizable element

some feature of the device user interface that can have its appearance altered, while retaining the same functionality

customization

a definition of the desired appearance changes to an element

customization policy

a mechanism that may prevent changing the contents of customizable elements with the API even if the necessary security permission is granted

DRM

Digital Rights Management

element group

a collection of elements with a shared feature and individual roles

feature

a high-level classification of some concept of a customizable user interface

file format compliant implementation

a partial implementation with support only for the file format and not the API

fully compliant implementation

a complete implementation of the Mobile User Interface Customization API and support for the file format

kind

the kind of some customizable element

lookup order

the order in which the element hierarchy is searched when looking for a particular element

modify operation

some operation that changes the content of an element

role

an identification of some customizable element's function within a feature

skin

an application-specific theme

skinnable application

an application that can have its user interface customized independently

skin name

identifying string for a skin in the format name:version:vendor

standalone element

a single standalone element with associated feature and role attributes and content

system default theme

the collection of default appearances for all the customizable elements supported by the implementation

theme

a collection of user interface customization data affecting the whole device

theme name

identifying string for a theme in the format name:version:vendor

toolkit element

a customizable element that belongs to some user interface toolkit implemented in the device, as opposed to a base element
